subjects.displayTitle: Prayer for nearness to God: longing that changes a life
subjects.introduction: What does it mean to ask for nearness to One who already sees and knows us? These prayers begin within that relationship, then open it through longing, thanksgiving, uncertainty and hope. A thirsty fish seeks the ocean; a leaf moves in the winds of divine will; the heart asks for a door to be opened and for the veils of its own desires to fall away. Such images invite reflection on a change of attention, understanding and conduct, while letters concerning journeys and prevented visits give the desire for presence a particular human setting. The neighboring subjects of nearness to God, prayer, and the presence of the Manifestation help us explore these dimensions together. Some passages speak through acute grief or suffering, whose circumstances deserve to be heard; others find in remembrance a daily rhythm, or ask that distance from home become a means of drawing other people nearer to God. The movement from I to we, and from one’s own need to another person’s well-being, gives the collection an expanding circle of concern. Psalm 139’s meditation on being known and Qur’an 2:186’s relationship between calling and responding offer further ways into its questions. Throughout, the prayer for nearness becomes inseparable from requests for guidance, steadfastness, contentment and the ability to serve: what kind of life might grow from learning to desire these together?
subjects.arc: Seen, known and drawn near → Grace already received → Turning throughout the day → The language of longing → Desire and the will of God → What hinders nearness → Recognition, hearing and the limits of knowledge → At the door of bounty → Presence, journeys and acceptance → Prayer that includes others → Sorrow, loss and the life to come → Nearness in every condition and world → The fruits of nearness

order.why: Begin with being seen and known before asking to draw near.
Let a brief plea for help interrupt the temptation to imagine the journey as self-sufficient.
Make uncertainty about what profits the supplicant an opening for knowledge and guidance.
Introduce the surprising images of broken wings and thirsty fish before the later petitions unfold them.
Answer the helpless fish with a prayer to swim by divine leave and will.
Introduce the outward consequence of inward longing: distance from home can help others draw near.

questions: How does the opening affirmation of being seen and known change the meaning of asking to draw near? Which later prayer brings a new dimension to that relationship?

What do the recurring images of thirst, fire, veils, doors, wings and oceans allow the prayers to express? Choose two images that pull your understanding in different directions and explore what each reveals.

How do the prayers hold personal longing together with uncertainty about what is best, contentment with divine will and the desire to act? What might change in the way a person prays when these are held together?
How do the passages about journeys, prevented visits, suffering and bereavement deepen the idea of presence? What becomes clearer when their particular circumstances remain in view?
What happens as the voice of prayer moves among I, we and prayers for another person? How might the request for nearness reshape service, family relationships or a community’s attention to others?

What new questions emerge beside Psalm 139 and Qur’an 2:186? Which connected subject—nearness to God, prayer more generally, or attaining God’s presence through the Manifestation—would help you explore them further?

references.label: 1 · Psalm 139:1–18 · Already known, still seeking
references.note: The psalm begins with the speaker already known by God, then asks where one could go beyond the divine presence. Distance and darkness fail to conceal the person who prays, and the reflection turns toward wonder at being formed and sustained. Read this beside the opening prayer and the collection’s requests to be drawn near. What might nearness mean when divine knowledge already encompasses a life? How do the psalm’s images of space and darkness converse with the prayers’ images of veils, recognition and orientation? Attend to each text’s particular voice as you explore their shared questions.
references.verified: Read Psalm139:1–18 in full, King James Version, Bible Gateway, 2026-10-10. Verified divine knowledge, presence beyond distance and darkness, formation and the final affirmation of being with God.

references.label: 2 · Qur’an 2:186 · Calling and responding
references.note: In this verse, the declaration of divine nearness accompanies a response to the person who calls; those addressed are also called to respond and believe, with guidance in view. Read the Sahih International translation, alongside the other translations provided. Compare the verse with prayers here that ask for help in remembering, obeying and serving. How does a petition become part of a relationship in which the supplicant also responds? What questions arise when longing, assurance and action are read together? The comparison invites attention to what each passage says about response, without prescribing the form an answer must take.
references.verified: Read the complete verse in the Quranic Arabic Corpus parallel primary translations, including explicitly labeled Sahih International, 2026-10-10. Verified nearness, response to invocation, the call for human response and belief, and guidance.
